summary: Specifies the ASN.X representation of encoding instructions for the XML Encoding Rules (XER). ASN.X is an XML representation of ASN.1 specifications. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: This is a companion note that shows how another set of encoding hints is written in the tidy XML format.

questions: how does asn.x represent xer instructions
what are target lists in xer encoding
subtitle: How to write encoding hints for XML structures in a structured XML notation.

tldr.problem: XER (XML Encoding Rules) is a comprehensive standard for encoding ASN.1 data as XML, with many encoding instructions to control XML generation. Each encoding rule set has its own notation, and XER's notation needed an ASN.X representation for translation to XML form.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4914 defines translation rules for mapping XER encoding instructions from ASN.1 to ASN.X. Each instruction type (Attribute, Element, Base64, Text, etc.) translates to a corresponding XML element with appropriate attributes and child elements. Target lists specify which parts of a data structure each instruction applies to.
tldr.outcome: Developers can express XER encoding instructions in ASN.X form, making ASN.1 specifications fully representable in XML while preserving all encoding control semantics.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ASN.X is an XML representation of ASN.1 specifications. This RFC specifies how encoding instructions for XER (XML Encoding Rules) are represented in ASN.X form. The XER standard itself defines how to encode ASN.1 values as XML, and its encoding instructions allow fine-grained control over that encoding process.

Unlike GSER (which has one instruction), XER provides 22 different encoding instruction types. Each can appear as a type prefix (applying to a single component) or in an encoding control section (applying to targeted components across the specification). This RFC defines the exact mapping of all 22 instruction types and the target selection mechanism from ASN.1 notation to ASN.X XML elements.
sections.eli5: ASN.X lets you write ASN.1 in XML. XER is a way to turn ASN.1 data into XML. This RFC shows how to move XER's control instructions from the text format to the XML format.

sections.title: XER Encoding Instructions Overview
sections.content:
XER defines encoding instructions in 22 categories, each controlling a specific aspect of XML encoding:

Basic structural choices: ATTRIBUTE (encode as XML attribute), ELEMENT (encode as child element), TEXT (embed text content), UNTAGGED (omit wrapper element), EMBED-VALUES (merge child elements into parent).

Data representation: BASE64 (use base64 encoding), DECIMAL (use decimal representation), LIST (encode sequence as space-separated values), USE-NUMBER (prefer numeric representation).

Naming and namespacing: NAME (specify XML element/attribute name), NAMESPACE (set namespace URI and prefix), GLOBAL-DEFAULTS (set encoding defaults for the module).

Advanced control: USE-UNION (select union member by type), USE-TYPE (use type information), USE-ORDER (preserve field order), USE-NIL (represent empty values as XML nil), USE-QNAME (use qualified names), DEFAULT-FOR-EMPTY (specify default for empty elements).

References and flexibility: ANY-ATTRIBUTES (allow arbitrary XML attributes), ANY-ELEMENT (allow arbitrary XML elements), PI-OR-COMMENT (insert processing instructions or comments), WHITESPACE (normalize whitespace).

Each instruction becomes an XML element when translated to ASN.X, preserving the instruction's parameters as child elements or attributes.
sections.eli5: These are like buttons on the XML encoder: 'use attributes instead of elements,' 'encode this as base64,' 'give this field a different name,' and so on. The RFC shows how to write each button in XML.

sections.title: Translation of Instructions to ASN.X
sections.content:
Each XER encoding instruction translates systematically to an ASN.X element. For example:

The ATTRIBUTE instruction becomes <attribute/> (an empty element).

The NAME instruction becomes <name> with either a newName attribute (for a custom name) or a conversion attribute (for case transformations like 'uncapitalized').

The NAMESPACE instruction becomes <namespace> with name and prefix attributes specifying the URI and XML prefix.

Instructions in encoding control sections become <targettedInstruction> elements. Each such element contains the instruction itself followed by <target> elements that specify which parts of the data structure the instruction applies to.

Target specifications can identify a type by name, a component by path (e.g., a/b/item), specific field identifiers in an ENUMERATED or INTEGER type, or even all types or all identifiers using 'ALL'.
sections.eli5: The translation is straightforward: each instruction type becomes an XML element with the same logical content, and instructions that apply to specific parts of the data get wrapped with information about which parts they target.

sections.title: Targeting Instructions to Data Elements
sections.content:
An important aspect of XER encoding instructions is target lists, which specify which parts of an ASN.1 data structure an instruction applies to. A target list can identify:

Types: A type name (optionally qualified with its module), or 'ALL' to mean all types in the module.

Components: A path through a structure, using solidus (/) separators. For example, a/b/item means the 'item' component type of a SEQUENCE OF inside component 'b' inside component 'a'.

Identifiers: Named values within ENUMERATED, INTEGER, or BIT STRING types, or 'ALL' to mean all such values.

Built-in types: References to types from the ASN.1 basic types.

When translating to ASN.X, a <target> element represents a single target. The type is specified in a type attribute, component paths appear in a <component> element, and identifiers appear in an <identifier> element. This allows encoding control sections to apply instructions selectively across the entire specification.
sections.eli5: Target lists are like address labels: 'apply this instruction to all fields named X,' 'apply to X's sub-field Y,' or 'apply to every integer field named Z throughout the spec.'

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
An ASN.X translation of XER encoding instructions is semantically equivalent to the original ASN.1 notation. An application built from the ASN.1 source has the same security properties as one built from the ASN.X translation.

The RFC defines preprocessing rules for cases where encoding instructions reference imported types. These rules ensure the ASN.X translation correctly represents the intended effects of the instructions.

RFC 4914 is an Experimental protocol from 2007 and remains experimental without updates or obsoletions.
sections.eli5: Whether you write the instructions in ASN.1 or in ASN.X, they mean the same thing and work the same way.
